title: Candidaemia and invasive candidiasis (adult)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Treat every Candida-positive blood culture: start an echinocandin, remove the central line, repeat cultures until negative, arrange a dilated eye examination, step down to fluconazole after 5 to 7 days if stable and susceptible, and treat for 14 days after the first negative culture.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Any Candida species in a blood culture is significant: never dismiss it as a contaminant.

Risk factors: central venous catheter, parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU stay, abdominal surgery or anastomotic leak, necrotising pancreatitis, dialysis, neutropenia, chemotherapy or transplant, multisite Candida colonisation.
Candida in sputum, catheter urine or surface swabs usually means colonisation and does not need antifungal treatment on its own.
In Indian ICUs C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis and C. auris are common and azole resistance is frequent, so species identification and susceptibility testing are essential.

sections.title: First steps
items: Start an echinocandin (IDSA 2016): caspofungin 70 mg IV loading then 50 mg daily, or micafungin 100 mg IV daily, or anidulafungin 200 mg IV loading then 100 mg daily.

Remove the central venous catheter as early as possible when it is the presumed source and removal is safe (non-neutropenic patients). In neutropenia, decide case by case, as the gut is a common source.
Repeat blood cultures daily or every other day until negative; the first negative culture starts the treatment clock.
Send the isolate for species identification and antifungal susceptibility testing.

sections.title: Look for complications
items: Dilated fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist within the first week in non-neutropenic patients, and after neutrophil recovery in neutropenic patients; endophthalmitis changes drug choice and duration.
Echocardiography if candidaemia persists, a prosthetic valve or cardiac device is present, or there is a new murmur.
Persistent candidaemia: look for a deep focus with abdominal imaging, Doppler ultrasound for septic thrombophlebitis, and bone or joint imaging if symptomatic.

sections.title: Step-down, species and duration
items: Step down to fluconazole 400 mg (6 mg/kg) orally daily, usually after 5 to 7 days, when clinically stable, the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible and repeat blood cultures are negative.

Fluconazole 800 mg (12 mg/kg) loading then 400 mg (6 mg/kg) daily is an acceptable initial alternative only for patients who are not critically ill and unlikely to have a fluconazole-resistant isolate (no recent azole exposure).

C. glabrata: step down only to fluconazole 800 mg (12 mg/kg) daily or voriconazole 200 to 300 mg (3 to 4 mg/kg) twice daily if susceptible. C. krusei: voriconazole step-down. C. parapsilosis: fluconazole is preferred once susceptibility is known.
Lipid amphotericin B 3 to 5 mg/kg IV daily if echinocandins are not tolerated or unavailable, or for resistant isolates.

Duration: 14 days after the first negative blood culture and resolution of symptoms, with no metastatic complications. Endophthalmitis, endocarditis and other deep foci need longer, specialist-guided courses.

sections.title: Candida auris
items: Treat invasive C. auris infection with an echinocandin at standard doses (CDC). Most isolates are fluconazole-resistant and some resist amphotericin B or echinocandins; if echinocandin-resistant, liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg IV daily with specialist advice.
Do not treat colonisation (screening swabs, urine or other non-invasive sites) without infection.
Conventional identification systems can misidentify C. auris; confirm with MALDI-TOF or molecular methods.

Infection control: single room with contact precautions, dedicated equipment, a disinfectant effective against C. auris, flag the record and inform infection control. Colonisation can persist indefinitely.

sections.title: Neutropenia, organ dysfunction and pregnancy
items: Neutropenic patients: an echinocandin or lipid amphotericin B first; step-down fluconazole 400 mg daily is acceptable if stable and susceptible. Treat for at least 14 days after clearance, once neutropenia has resolved.
Renal impairment: halve the fluconazole maintenance dose if creatinine clearance is 50 mL/min or less; echinocandins need no renal adjustment.
Hepatic impairment: reduce caspofungin maintenance to 35 mg daily in moderate impairment.
Pregnancy: avoid fluconazole, especially at high dose and in the first trimester; lipid amphotericin B is preferred; seek specialist advice.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating Candida in blood as a contaminant, or stopping before 14 days after clearance.
Leaving the central line in place.
Starting fluconazole empirically in an unstable patient or after recent azole exposure.
Skipping the eye examination.
Treating Candida in sputum or catheter urine as invasive infection.

drugs.name: Caspofungin
drugs.dose: 70 mg IV loading, then 50 mg IV once daily
drugs.notes: First line. 35 mg maintenance in moderate hepatic impairment.

drugs.name: Anidulafungin
drugs.dose: 200 mg IV loading, then 100 mg IV once daily
drugs.notes: First line; no hepatic or renal adjustment.

drugs.name: Fluconazole
drugs.dose: 800 mg (12 mg/kg) loading, then 400 mg (6 mg/kg) orally or IV once daily; C. glabrata step-down 800 mg (12 mg/kg) daily
drugs.notes: Step-down for susceptible isolates. Halve maintenance if creatinine clearance 50 mL/min or less. Many drug interactions; QT prolongation.

drugs.name: Voriconazole
drugs.dose: 400 mg (6 mg/kg) twice daily for 2 doses, then 200 to 300 mg (3 to 4 mg/kg) twice daily
drugs.notes: C. krusei or susceptible C. glabrata step-down. Therapeutic drug monitoring; visual and hepatic toxicity.

drugs.name: Lipid amphotericin B
drugs.notes: Intolerance or resistance; echinocandin-resistant C. auris 5 mg/kg (liposomal). Monitor potassium, magnesium and creatinine.
